{{CS1 config|mode=cs1}}
In [[number theory]], a [[positive integer]] {{mvar|k}} is said to be an '''Erdős–Woods number''' if it has the following property:
there exists a positive integer {{mvar|a}} such that in the [[sequence]] {{math|(''a'', ''a'' + 1, …, ''a'' + ''k'')}} of consecutive integers, each of the elements has a non-trivial [[common factor]] with one of the endpoints.  In other words, {{mvar|k}} is an Erdős–Woods number if there exists a positive integer {{mvar|a}} such that for each integer {{mvar|i}} between {{math|0}} and {{mvar|k}}, at least one of the [[greatest common divisor]]s {{math|gcd(''a'', ''a'' + ''i'')}}  or {{math|gcd(''a'' + ''i'', ''a'' + ''k'')}} is greater than {{math|1}}.

==Examples==
[[16 (number)|16]] is an Erdős–Woods number because the 15 numbers between 2184 and {{nowrap|1=2200 = 2184 + 16}} each share a [[prime factor]] with one of {{nowrap|1=2184 = 2<sup>3</sup> &middot; 3 &middot; 7 &middot; 13}} and
{{nowrap|1=2200 = 2<sup>3</sup> &middot; 5<sup>2</sup> &middot; 11.}} These 15 numbers and their shared prime factor(s) are:
{{bi|left=1.6|1=<table class=wikitable>
<tr>
<td> 2185<br/> 5</td>
<td> 2186<br/> 2</td>
<td> 2187<br/> 3</td>
<td> 2188<br/> 2</td>
<td> 2189<br/> 11</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td> 2190<br/> 2, 3, 5</td>
<td> 2191<br/> 7</td>
<td> 2192<br/> 2</td>
<td> 2193<br/> 3</td>
<td> 2194<br/> 2</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td> 2195<br/> 5</td>
<td> 2196<br/> 2, 3</td>
<td> 2197<br/> 13</td>
<td> 2198<br/> 2, 7</td>
<td> 2199<br/> 3</td>
</tr>
</table>}}

The first Erdős–Woods numbers are
{{bi|left=1.6|[[16 (number)|16]], [[22 (number)|22]], [[34 (number)|34]], [[36 (number)|36]], [[46 (number)|46]], [[56 (number)|56]], [[64 (number)|64]], [[66 (number)|66]], [[70 (number)|70]], [[76 (number)|76]], [[78 (number)|78]], [[86 (number)|86]], [[88 (number)|88]], [[92 (number)|92]], [[94 (number)|94]], [[96 (number)|96]], [[100]], [[106 (number)|106]], [[112 (number)|112]], [[116 (number)|116]] … {{OEIS|id=A059756}}.}}
Although all of these initial numbers are even, odd Erdős–Woods numbers also exist. They include
{{bi|left=1.6|903, 2545, 4533, 5067, 8759, 9071, 9269, 10353, 11035, 11625, 11865, 13629, 15395, ... {{OEIS|A111042}}.}}

==Prime partitions==
The Erdős–Woods numbers can be characterized in terms of certain partitions of the [[prime number]]s. A number {{mvar|k}} is an Erdős–Woods number if and only if the prime numbers less than {{mvar|k}} can be partitioned into two subsets {{mvar|X}} and {{mvar|Y}} with the following property: for every pair of positive integers {{mvar|x}} and {{mvar|y}} with {{math|1=''x'' + ''y'' = ''k''}}, either {{mvar|x}} is divisible by a prime in {{mvar|X}}, or {{mvar|y}} is divisible by a prime in {{mvar|Y}}. For this reason, these numbers are also called ''prime-partitionable numbers''.{{r|oeis}}

For instance, 16 is prime-partitionable with {{math|1=''X'' = {3, 7, 13}}} and {{math|1=''Y'' = {2, 5, 11}}}.{{r|hs}} The representations of 16 as {{math|''x'' + ''y''}} and corresponding prime divisors in {{mvar|X}} and {{mvar|Y}} are:
{{bi|left=1.6|1=<table class=wikitable>
<tr style="vertical-align:top;">
<td> 1 + 15<br/> 5 {{pipe}} {{mvar|y}}</td>
<td> 2 + 14<br/> 2 {{pipe}} {{mvar|y}}</td>
<td> 3 + 13<br/> 3 {{pipe}} {{mvar|x}}</td>
<td> 4 + 12<br/> 2 {{pipe}} {{mvar|y}}</td>
<td> 5 + 11<br/> 11 {{pipe}} {{mvar|y}}</td>
</tr>
<tr style="vertical-align:top;">
<td> 6 + 10<br/>3 {{pipe}} {{mvar|x}}<br/> 2, 5 {{pipe}} {{mvar|y}}</td>
<td> 7 + 9<br/> 7 {{pipe}} {{mvar|x}}</td>
<td> 8 + 8<br/> 2 {{pipe}} {{mvar|y}}</td>
<td> 9 + 7<br/> 3 {{pipe}} {{mvar|x}}</td>
<td> 10 + 6<br/> 2 {{pipe}} {{mvar|y}}</td>
</tr>
<tr style="vertical-align:top;">
<td> 11 + 5<br/> 5 {{pipe}} {{mvar|y}}</td>
<td> 12 + 4<br/>3 {{pipe}} {{mvar|x}}<br/> 2 {{pipe}} {{mvar|y}}</td>
<td> 13 + 3<br/> 13 {{pipe}} {{mvar|x}}</td>
<td> 14 + 2<br/> 7 {{pipe}} {{mvar|x}}<br/> 2 {{pipe}} {{mvar|y}}</td>
<td> 15 + 1<br/> 3 {{pipe}} {{mvar|x}}</td>
</tr>
</table>}}

==History==
In a 1971 paper, [[Paul Erdős]] and [[John Selfridge]] considered intervals of integers containing an element coprime to both endpoints. They observed that earlier results of [[Subbayya Sivasankaranarayana Pillai|S. S. Pillai]] and [[George Szekeres]] implied that such an element exists for every interval of at most 16 integers; thus, no Erdős–Woods number can be less than 16.{{r|es}} In his 1981 thesis, Alan R. Woods independently conjectured{{r|woods}} that whenever {{math|''k''&nbsp;>&nbsp;1}}, the interval {{math|[''a'', ''a'' + ''k'']}} always includes a number [[coprime]] to both endpoints. It was only later that he found the first counterexample, {{math|[2184, 2185, …, 2200]}}, with {{math|1=''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;16}}. The existence of this counterexample shows that 16 is an Erdős–Woods number.{{r|dowe}} {{harvtxt|Dowe|1989}} proved that there are infinitely many Erdős–Woods numbers,{{r|dowe}} and {{harvtxt|Cégielski|Heroult|Richard|2003}} showed that the [[Set (mathematics)|set]] of Erdős–Woods numbers is [[recursive set|recursive]].{{r|chr}}

Meanwhile, the prime-partitionable numbers had been defined by Holsztyński and Strube in 1978,{{r|hs}} following which Erdős and [[William T. Trotter]] proved in 1978 that they form an infinite sequence. Erdős and Trotter applied these results to generate pairs of [[directed cycle]]s whose [[Cartesian product of graphs]] does not contain a [[Hamiltonian cycle]], and they used a computer search to find several odd prime-partitionable numbers, including 15395 and 397197.{{r|te}} In 2014, M. F. Hasler observed on the [[On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences]] that the prime-partitionable numbers appeared to be the same as the Erdős–Woods numbers, and this was proven in the same year by Christopher Hunt Gribble.{{r|oeis}} The same equivalence was also shown by Hasler and Mathar in 2015, together with an equivalence between two definitions of the prime-partitionable numbers from the two earlier works on the subject.{{r|hm}}
